items.title: 'गंगा-जमुनी' फ़ैंटेसी, मिटती भाषाएं एवं सोशल मीडिया के दौर में यूनिवर्सिटीज़ और लोकतंत्र का भविष्य
items.summary: प्रोफेसर अली खान महमूदाबाद अपनी किताब ‘पोएट्री ऑफ़ बिलॉन्गिंग’ में लिखते हैं कि कैसे भारत के मुसलमानों ने ऐतिहासिक रूप से इस सरज़मीन से अपना जुड़ाव केवल किसी नक्शे या राज्य की राजनीतिक सीमाओं के ज़रिए नहीं, बल्कि यहां की संस्कृति, शायरी और सांझी विरासत के ज़रिए महसूस किया. लेकिन आज के मीडिया और राजनीति के इस दौर में, जहां वफ़ादारी और देशभक्ति का इम्तिहान रोज़ प्राइमटाइम टीवी और सोशल मीडिया पर लिया जाता है, अपनेपन का वह ख़याल आख़िर कहां खो गया है? न्यूज़लॉन्ड्री इंटरव्यूज के इस ख़ास एपिसोड में हमने प्रोफ़ेसर अली खान महमूदाबाद से बात की. प्रोफ़ेसर खान अशोका यूनिवर्सिटी में राजनीतिक विज्ञान विभाग के प्रमुख हैं, एक जाने-माने इतिहासकार, लेखक और समाजशास्त्र के गहरे जानकार हैं. कैम्ब्रिज यूनिवर्सिटी से पीएचडी करने वाले प्रोफेसर खान की रिसर्च दक्षिण एशिया में पहचान, नागरिकता और ऐतिहासिक यादों के ताने-बाने को बहुत गहराई से समझती है. आज के भारत में जहां इतिहास को नए सिरे से लिखा जा रहा है, विश्वविद्यालयों में आज़ाद सोच और बहस की जगहें सिकुड़ रही हैं, और सोशल मीडिया पर ट्रॉलिंग के ज़रिए राजनीति की दिशा तय हो रही है, वहां एक अकादमिक और संजीदा आवाज़ की क्या जगह बचती है? इस इंटरव्यू में प्रोफ़ेसर खान ने अवध की लखनवी तहज़ीब, गंगा-जमुनी संस्कृति की प्रचलित अवधारणाओं, भाषा (उर्दू और हिंदी) के अस्तित्व के संकट और डिजिटल दौर में बदलती इंसानी पहचान पर बेबाक विचार रखे. अपनी पारिवारिक विरासत, महमूदाबाद की ऐतिहासिक रियासत और दुर्लभ पांडुलिपियों के संग्रह पर बात करते हुए प्रोफ़ेसर खान ने कहा कि पूंजीवाद के इस दौर में सांस्कृतिक और ऐतिहासिक धरोहरों का व्यावसायीकरण एक कड़वी सच्चाई बन चुका है, लेकिन इल्म सार्वजनिक संपत्ति होना चाहिए. उन्होंने स्पष्ट किया कि वे अपनी पारिवारिक लाइब्रेरी में मौजूद दुर्लभ पांडुलिपियों और पुरानी किताबों को एक ओपन डिजिटल रीडिंग रूम में बदलने की कोशिश कर रहे हैं ताकि दुनिया के किसी भी कोने में बैठा व्यक्ति उन्हें मुफ़्त में पढ़ सके. उनका मानना है कि सदियों पहले किसी लेखक द्वारा लिखे गए ज्ञान पर किसी एक व्यक्ति या परिवार का एकाधिकार या ताला नहीं होना चाहिए. अवध की संस्कृति और भाईचारे पर बात करते हुए उन्होंने पारंपरिक 'गंगा-जमुनी तहज़ीब' की आधुनिक व्याख्या पर सवाल उठाया. प्रोफ़ेसर खान के अनुसार आजकल गंगा-जमुनी तहज़ीब को इस तरह पेश किया जाता है मानो उसमें धर्म का घोल था यानी हिंदू और मुसलमान अपने धर्मों से दूर होकर लिबरल बने और साथ रहने लगे. इसे उन्होंने एक पोस्ट-कोलोनियल सेक्युलर एलीट फ़ैंटेसी करार दिया. उनका कहना है कि असलियत यह थी कि लोग अपने-अपने धर्म और आस्था में बेहद मज़बूत रहकर भी एक-दूसरे की धार्मिक और सांस्कृतिक सीमाओं का सम्मान करते हुए साथ रहते थे. भारत में सामाजिक भाईचारा धर्म से दूर हटकर नहीं, बल्कि धर्म की गहरी जड़ों के भीतर से ही निकला था. आज की

items.title: Ali Khan Mahmudabad on ‘Ganga-Jamuni fantasy’, dying languages and democracy online
items.summary: In this Newslaundry interview, Professor Ali Khan Mahmudabad, head of Political Science at Ashoka University and author of Poetry of Belonging , examines how culture, poetry and shared histories have shaped Indian Muslims’ relationship with the country, and what threatens that sense of belonging today. From calling the popular idea of Ganga-Jamuni tehzeeb a “postcolonial secular elite fantasy” to warning about the erosion of Hindi and Urdu, Professor Khan challenges familiar narratives about religion, secularism and social harmony. He argues that people did not have to abandon their faiths to live together; they built bonds while remaining deeply rooted in their own religious traditions. He also discusses the rewriting of history, shrinking space for dissent in universities, and how social media is reshaping identity and political discourse. As trolling becomes routine and politics increasingly plays out online, what is at stake for India’s democracy? The conversation also turns to the political scientist’s lineage, the historic estate of Mahmudabad and its rare manuscripts. Professor Khan argues that knowledge should be a public good, not a family possession, and is working to make his family’s collection freely accessible through an open digital reading room. Watch the full conversation on the myths surrounding India’s shared culture, the future of its languages, academic freedom, and what remains of Awadh’s famed tehzeeb .

items.title: South Central 97: Why were journalists being detained and beaten by Delhi Police?
items.summary: Were the police only trying to stop the protests, or also to stop journalists from creating a public record of what happened on the streets? What happens when journalists covering protests are detained by the police, and what does it mean for press freedom and the right to dissent in India? In this week’s South Central, hosts Dhanya Rajendran and Anisha Sheth examine the crackdown’s implications for independent media, press freedom and the right to protest. They are joined by Siddharth Varadarajan, founding editor of The Wire , and Abhinandan Sekhri of Newslaundry , to discuss allegations of police violence, the targeting of journalists documenting the protests, and the lack of a stronger collective response from mainstream media. The discussion examines whether the police were not only trying to prevent protests but also attempting to stop journalists from creating a public record of what happened on the streets. Siddharth Varadarajan argues that journalists documenting police action during earlier protests had brought evidence of violence and excessive force to public attention, and that reporters were targeted this time to prevent similar footage from reaching audiences. Independent media journalists, including younger and women reporters, were among those who faced rough treatment and detention. The panel also discusses allegations of violence against protesters and journalists inside detention centres, the role of people accompanying the police in confronting demonstrators, and the response of mainstream media to the detentions. In the second part of the episode, the hosts speak to TNM Associate Editor Sukanya Shaji about the crash near Kochi airport in Kerala in which three young people were killed after a Mini Cooper reportedly driven at high speed rammed into their scooter. The 19-year-old driver was arrested and booked for culpable homicide not amounting to murder, prompting questions about the legal provisions applied in the case. The discussion also examines allegations of rash and drunken driving, reports that the driver or a passenger claimed his father would take care of the situation, and the wider debate around privilege and accountability. The panel looks at the victim-blaming that followed the crash, particularly questions about why the two women were out late at night with a Muslim male friend. items.title: Delhi High Court says no need to disclose records of foreign travel in IAF aircraft by PM, ex-PM
items.summary: The Delhi High Court has set aside a Central Information Commission (CIC) order directing Indian Air Force to disclose detailed records relating to Prime Minister (PM) Narendra Modi and former PM Manmohan Singh’s foreign travel under the Right to Information Act (RTI Act). Justice Amit Mahajan noted that the RTI applicant, retired Commodore Lokesh Batra, had sought details about Special Flight Returns (SFR) Part I & Part II, which include details of aircraft, aircrew, the entire entourage, including names of all the Special Protection Group (SPG) personnel travelling with the PM. The Court observed that providing this information could compromise national security and endanger the PM's life and physical safety. “The potential implications of such disclosure for national security and the security apparatus accompanying the Hon’ble Prime Minister cannot be disregarded,” the High Court said in its October 15 order. Justice Amit Mahajan, Delhi High Court Justice Mahajan ruled that the High Court or the CIC “cannot sit in appeal over the subjective satisfaction of the competent security agencies as to whether disclosure of particular information could jeopardise national security or endanger the life and physical safety of the Hon’ble Prime Minister”. “Such an assessment falls primarily within the domain of the agencies entrusted with the responsibility of ensuring the security of the Hon’ble Prime Minister and this Court cannot substitute its own assessment for that of the competent security agencies,” the Court said. The case arose from an RTI application filed in June 2018 by retired Commodore Lokesh K Batra. He sought details of foreign visits undertaken by Indian Prime Ministers on Indian Air Force aircraft between April 2013 to June 2018 While the Air Force provided information about certain visits, it refused to disclose SFR Part-I and Part-II details. The Central Public Information Officer (CPIO) of the Air Force cited security concerns and also invoked the exemption for information held in a fiduciary capacity. However, the CIC directed the Air Force to provide certified copies of available and relevant SFR-II records after redacting the names of security personnel. This prompted the CPIO to approach the High Court. items.title: CJP's Saurav Das, Ashutosh Ranka to remain in jail as Delhi court extends their judicial custody
items.summary: A Special Executive Magistrate (SEM) court on Monday extended the judicial custody of Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) activists Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka by two days. Das and Ranka were detained by the Delhi Police on October 13 after they allegedly entered the barricaded Jantar Mantar site by climbing its gates. On October 14, they were sent to judicial custody for five days. As the custody ended today, they were produced before the SEM. The Delhi Police sought an extension of the custody. The same was allowed and the custody was extended by two more days. The CJP has been protesting alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls and demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.

items.title: Social media users must be given copy of takedown order: Punjab and Haryana High Court
items.summary: The Punjab and Haryana High Court recently said that authorities ordering takedown of a social media page must also inform the user while notifying the intermediary [Haryana 24 News Network Private Limited v Union of India and Others] Justice Tribhuvan Dahiya made the observation while setting aside an order passed by the Haryana Police directing takedown of the Facebook page of Haryana 24 News Network Private Limited. The Court noted that Rule 3(2) of the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 does not explicitly lay down the requirement to notify the user whose content or page is ordered to be taken down by the authorities. However, it observed that this requirement is an essential obligation ingrained in the principles of natural justice and has to be read into the rule. “Accordingly, a copy of the intimation must be furnished to the user when it is sent to the intermediary. This will make the procedure of sub-rule (2) to Rule 3 compliant of the primary tenets of natural justice and constitutionally valid,” the Court said. Justice Tribhuvan Dahiya The judgement was passed on a petition moved by Haryana 24 News Network Private Limited against the blocking of its Facebook page in India on the directions of Superintendent of Police of Yamuna Nagar. The petitioner told the Court no notice was given before blocking the Facebook page. In response, the police said one of the directors of the petitioner company is an accused in an extortion case and was using the Facebook page to intimidate the victim. Therefore, an intimation was issued to Facebook to disable the Facebook page. In the judgment passed on October 5, the Court said the officer authorised to issue such intimation cannot be below the rank of a Deputy Inspector General of Police (DIGP). Since the intimation in this case was issued by the Superintendent of Police, the Court found it to be in violation of the rules. It rejected the State government’s contention that the SP had been delegated the power to issue the intimation to the intermediary. The Court said that the State failed to point out the provision allowing such delegation. “Thus, it is evident that the Superintendent of Police usurped the power not vested in him in issuing the said intimation in flagrant violation of statutory provisions; this is sheer highhandedness and arbitrary exercise of power,” it ruled. items.title: Karnataka High Court upholds validity of law restricting construction around ancient, protected monuments
items.summary: The Karnataka High Court recently upheld the constitutional validity of amendments made in 2010 to the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act, 1958, that regulate constructions in areas surrounding centrally protected monuments [ BR Ramakrishna v. Union of India & others ]. By an October 9 ruling, Justice MGS Kamal rejected a challenge to Sections 20A, 20B and 20C of the Act by Tumkur resident BR Ramakrishna, who contended that the restrictions on construction within prohibited areas were arbitrary and unconstitutional. “Considering the object and purport of the Act and the constitutional mandate of Article 49 (protecting monuments) of the Constitution of India said classification cannot be found to be unreasonable, ambiguous or vague and unconnected as sought to be contended by the counsel for the petitioner. In any event, the reason and logic behind such classification falls within the expert domain of concerned competent authority under the Act, 1958," the Court held. Justice MG Shukure kamal Ramakrishna had challenged these provisions after he was refused permission to build a residential building on a plot of land he owned near Madhugiri Fort. In 2016, the Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) refused to grant permission for the construction, stating that the site was 59 metres away from the monument which was inside a prohibited 100 metre zone where no construction is allowed. This prompted Ramakrishna to challenge the validity of the law prescribing such restrictions on constructions near monuments. He contended that they violated his constitutional rights and that there was no scientific basis for the manner in which the no-construction zones were prescribed. In a report filed before the Court, the ASI expressed concern that the proposed construction could adversely affect the fort's aesthetic view and cultural landscape. It also apprehended that granting permission could prompt similar requests from other property owners in the vicinity. The Court eventually ruled that Ramakrishna had not discharged the burden cast on him to prove his claim that the provisions he challenged were unconstitutional. “Rejection of permission to put up construction in furtherance of a statute, which is regulatory in nature, cannot be the ground to quash, set aside, and declare the statute unconstitutional, particularly when the party seeking such annulment has not discharged the burden cast on him," it held. items.title: CJI Surya Kant announces special bench for hearing Ladakh cases pending in Supreme Court
items.summary: Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant on Sunday announced that he would set up a special bench of the Supreme Court to hear cases from Ladakh pending before the top court. CJI Kant was speaking at the inaugural function of the Ladakh bench of the Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh High Court . “I will certainly make an arrangement to set up a special bench on one day to hear all cases from the Ladakh region that are pending before the Supreme Court,” CJI Kant said. CJI Kant, however, said the cases should be argued by lawyers from Leh and Kargil. He added that advocates could appear online before the bench from the Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh High Court's bench in Leh. “The reason is very obvious. I want that every member of the Kargil and Leh bar must feel integrated with this Supreme Court and Supreme Court bar, and you must feel that you don't represent this area alone. You are in fact representative of the bar association of India, and I can say with again assurance that your competence, your ability, and your articulation is as good as members of the Supreme Court bar. Therefore, you are not lagging behind in any manner in providing best of the assistance to us,” the CJI said. CJI Kant made the announcement while responding to Attorney General for India R Venkatramani 's suggestion that a Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court should one day sit and hold proceedings in Ladakh's calm environment, away from the "noisy scenes" witnessed in Delhi. “When I saw two courts here, I also had this feeling that I should shift the Supreme Court here only. The courtrooms are so good!,” CJI Kant said. items.title: CJI Surya Kant inaugurates J&K High Court's Ladakh bench in Leh
items.summary: Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant on Sunday inaugurated Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh High Court's newly constituted Ladakh bench in Leh. Supreme Court Justices MM Sundresh , PS Narasimha and Arun Palli , along with judges of the High Court, were also present on the occasion. Attorney General for India R Venkatramani and Ladakh Lieutenant Governor VK Saxena also attended the event. Ladakh bench inauguration - Group photo Hearing of cases at the Ladakh bench will commence from October 21. A division bench of Chief Justice Pushpendra Singh Bhati and Justice Sanjay Parihar is expected to take up five cases on Wednesday. Justice Parihar will also preside over a single bench and hear cases on Thursday and Friday as well. The High Court has identified a total of 75 cases for listing before the bench situated in Leh. The Union government had approved the establishment of the Ladakh bench for the High Court of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh in August this year. Following the decision, the High Court on October 5 selected Leh as the place for holding sittings of the High Court in the Union Territory of Ladakh. Before the establishment of the Ladakh bench, the High Court had two benches at Srinagar and Jammu. Ladakh bench will be part of the High Court of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh, as it currently serves both Union Territories of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh. Ladakh was carved out as a separate Union Territory in 2019 following the reorganisation of the erstwhile State of Jammu and Kashmir. The decision to establish a bench in Ladakh is aimed at bringing High Court services closer to litigants in Ladakh, where geographical distances can make access to judicial institutions more difficult. items.title: Courting Controversy: Green becomes the new Gold: India’s Carbon Market opens for business
items.summary: As Diwali approaches and Delhi braces for its annual smog season, conversations about air quality usually turn to firecrackers and stubble burning. These conversations seem to miss out on pollution caused by factories, power plants and furnaces that run all year and are a steadier source of pollution. This is a fitting moment to ask what India’s biggest industrial emitters have been doing, and how the 2026 UN Climate Change COP31 will bring about an environmental change for the better. Starting November, for the first time, Indian factories will be able to buy and sell carbon credit certificates on power exchanges, finally turning a carbon credit trading scheme which was notified by the government in 2023, into a working market reality. The legal foundation for the concept is the Energy Conservation (Amendment) Act, 2022, which empowered the government to create an Indian carbon market and a carbon credit trading scheme which was notified in 2023 . The Bureau of Energy Efficiency has issued emission targets to around 490 industrial units across seven sectors and credits are expected to be issued this month, with trading between November and January. To understand this better how the carbon credit market works, think back to school. Imagine a school where every student gets a fixed number of late passes each term. The punctual kids end up with spares and the chronic latecomers run short. Now let them trade. The early birds sell their extras, the sleepyheads buy them, and the school still meets its overall punctuality target. Replace late passes with tonnes of carbon dioxide and students with factories, and what you have is carbon credit trading. The idea is simple. A government sets emission targets for polluting industries. A company that beats its target earns certain credits, one for every tonne of carbon dioxide it avoided. A company that misses must buy credits from the one who met its targets . Therefore, pollution gets a price tag, and environment friendly industry practices becomes a way of earning money instead of a cost. items.title: Mere presence not an offence: Delhi High Court quashes FIR against protestor in 2025 SSC demonstrations
items.summary: Mere presence at a protest venue beyond permitted hours does not constitute an offence, the Delhi High Court recently held while quashing an FIR registered against a competitive examination aspirant who participated in a demonstration at Ramlila Maidan concerning Staff Selection Commission (SSC) exams. [Khurshid Ahmed v. State of NCT of Delhi] Justice Sanjeev Narula allowed the petition filed by Khurshid Ahmed seeking the quashing of an FIR registered at Kamla Market police station under Sections 223(a) (disobedience to order promulgated by public servant) and 3(5) (common intention) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS). Justice Sanjeev Narula According to the prosecution, around 800 to 1,000 aspirants assembled at Ramlila Maidan on August 24, 2025. While permission was granted only until 5 pm, several protesters stayed back in violation of prohibitory orders issued under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS). It was alleged that protesters scuffled with police personnel, leading to the detention of 44 individuals, including Ahmed. Ahmed sought an urgent hearing before the High Court, submitting that he had cleared the recruitment examination for the Eklavya Model Residential School and needed to appear for document verification. He contended that he was neither an organiser nor a speaker, and was implicated merely due to his presence at the venue. The Court observed that mere disobedience of an order is insufficient; it must also cause or tend to cause obstruction, annoyance, or injury to public servants. “His mere presence amongst the protesters cannot, without more, be treated as sufficient to establish the offence,” the Court observed. The Court further held that the prosecution failed to establish common intention under Section 3(5) of the BNS. “The principle of common intention requires that the criminal act be committed in furtherance of an intention shared by the persons sought to be held jointly liable. Mere participation in the same demonstration does not, by itself, establish a common intention to disobey lawful directions or obstruct police personnel,” the bench noted. items.title: Imran Khan moves Bombay High Court against FRRO's ‘Leave India’ notice; flags procedural lapses
items.summary: Bollywood actor Imran Khan has approached the Bombay High Court challenging the notice issued by the Foreigners Regional Registration Office (FRRO) which directs him to leave the country by October 28 for allegedly violating the Foreigners Act. [Imran Khan Pal v. Union of India & Ors] In his petition, Khan has contended that executive authorities gave him no prior hearing, bypassed his statutory rights as an Overseas Citizen of India (OCI), and acted in hasty response to political social media campaigns. The American national was directed by FRRO to leave the country by October 28. This was after he was briefly detained by the police after taking part in demonstrations against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. The directive was issued shortly after Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) leader Kirit Somaiya filed an FIR at the Gamdevi police station alleging public-order infractions under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. On October 17, FRRO issued a show cause notice asking Khan why his OCI registration should not be cancelled under Section 7D of the Citizenship Act. According to the plea, Khan has lived in India for more than four decades with an Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) registration since 2006. The plea also highlights the unusual haste in issuing the expulsion directive. Khan has alleged that authorities acted under pressure from public social media campaigns by political functionaries rather than an independent application of mind. "Directing a lifelong resident to leave India on account of a brief and unjust detention, from which he was released the same evening, is wholly disproportionate," the plea states. Khan has also contended that the notice fails to identify the specific provision breached, the offending act or the timeline of the alleged contravention. items.title: UAPA no blanket bar on foreign travel: Delhi High Court allows riots accused Natasha Narwal to go to UK for PhD
items.summary: The Delhi High Court has allowed Delhi riots accused Natasha Narwal to travel to the United Kingdom for academic purposes and to meet her PhD supervisors. Justice Amit Bansal passed the order on October 16 and set aside the trial court order of October 6, which had denied her permission. While passing the order, the Court said that a case under the Unlawful Activities Prevention Act (UAPA) will not act as a blanket bar on a person's right to travel abroad. “The fact that the petitioner has been charged of serious offences under the UAPA does not curtail her right to travel abroad in a blanket manner,” the High Court observed in its order. Therefore, the Court allowed her to travel on a personal bond of ₹1 lakh with her brother as surety. Justice Bansal further said she will not seek asylum in the UK or comment on the cases against her. Justice Amit Bansal Narwal is pursuing PhD from University of Warwick and sought permission to attend an international academic conference in London, where her research paper, Gendered Carceral Labour as Social Reproduction, has been accepted for presentation. She also sought permission to meet her PhD supervisors and participate in academic activities at the university. The State opposed her request, arguing that she could pursue her academic engagements via video conference and that travelling to UK could pose difficulties if she seeks asylum there. After considering the case, the High Court noted that Narwal had been pursuing her doctorate remotely since her admission in October 2023 and that her supervisors had specifically invited her for in-person meetings, doctoral training and research activities. The Court observed that the trials were likely to take considerable time to conclude and that there was no allegation that she had violated any bail conditions since being granted bail. Therefore, it allowed her request to travel. Advocates Adit S Pujari, Chaitanya Sundriyal, Manvender Singh Shekhawat and Harshvardhan Pushkin Sharma appeared for Natasha Narwal. Additional Solicitor General (ASG) SV Raju , Special Public Prosecutors (SPP) Madhukar Pandey and Ayodhya Prasad with advocates Dhruv Pande, Aarush Bhatia, Saravjeet Singh and Ishika Singla represented the Delhi Police. items.title: Mini Cooper crash: Kerala court denies bail to accused Suhail Sajeev and 3 others
items.summary: A Kerala court on Saturday denied bail to Suhail Sajeev and three others, booked in connection with the Mini Cooper car accident which led to the death of three motorcyclists. Sajeev along with Ninav, Joel and Ameer had filed bail applications before a trial court in Angamaly. However, Judicial First Class Magistrate Samyuktha MK dismissed their bail pleas. The case stemmed from an accident which happened on October 11 when a Mini Cooper driven by Sajeev at high speed hit a scooter carrying three youngsters on the Athani-Airport Road in Nedumbassery, killing all three. According to the First Information Report (FIR), the impact threw all three onto the road, causing severe injuries to their heads and bodies. While two of them died on the spot, the third succumbed to injuries later. The Nedumbassery Airport Police Station registered a case under Section 105 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), which deals with culpable homicide not amounting to murder. The police subsequently arrested Sajeev and three others in connection with the incident. The three were riding in the car along with Sajeev, who was behind the wheel. All four accused were remanded to 14 days of judicial custody on October 14. According to reports , Sajeev was driving under the influence of alcohol at the time of the incident. During the bail hearing on October 16, the counsel appearing for the accused argued that the incident only amounted to rash and negligent driving rather than culpable homicide. It was also argued that the victims too had violated the traffic rules as all three of them were riding on a scooter while using the middle lane of the road. The abetment charges against the other three accused were challenged on the ground that they had only accompanied Sajeev in the car. However, the prosecution and the victim's counsel opposed the bail plea, arguing that the accident could not be treated as an ordinary case of negligent driving. CCTV footage was relied upon to show that all the accused had visited several bars and were inebriated before the accident. It was also alleged that the co-accused in the car had encouraged Sajeev to drive, despite knowing that he was drunk. The Court today dismissed the bail pleas. Advocates Saiby Jose Kidangoor, Sreeraj S Rajaram and Afsana Khan appeared for Sajeev. items.title: PIL in Calcutta High Court seeks double-side printing on A4 paper for pleadings in West Bengal courts
items.summary: A Public Interest Litigation (PIL) has been filed before the Calcutta High Court seeking a uniform mandate for filing physical pleadings and documents in 75 GSM A4 paper in duplex (back-to-back) format in the High Court and other courts across West Bengal [Akash Sharma v. Registrar General, High Court at Calcutta and Another] . The PIL aims to lower paper consumption, printing services and costs and the physical bulk of court records. The case is listed for hearing on November 23. Calcutta High Court on February 22, 2021 had asked its administrative side to consider mandating use of A4 paper with double-side printing for pleadings and filings. However, the plea filed by advocate Akash Sharma states that further progress of the matter could not be ascertained through publicly available records or notices. This PIL primarily seeks to determine the outcome of the order dated February 22, 2021 and a fresh consideration of the matter to prescribe a uniform practice of using 75 GSM A4 paper in a duplex-printed format across all courts in the State. items.title: Alliance Air pays over ₹16 lakh to 33 passengers after consumer court issues NBW over flight cancellation
items.summary: Over two years after abruptly cancelling a Hyderabad–Mysore flight, Alliance Air has cleared more than ₹16 lakh in compensation to 33 passengers following the issuance of non-bailable warrants by a Hyderabad consumer commission [Radha Devi Mandhana vs M/s The Alliance Aviation Ltd]. The District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission-II, Hyderabad, comprising President Vakkanti Narasimha Rao and Members P V T R Jawahar Babu and Suma Vala , terminated execution proceedings on October 14 after recording satisfaction of the decree. The Bench also recalled the non-bailable warrants (NBWs) previously issued against airline officials. The dispute arose from an incident on June 2, 2022, when a 33-member family group, including senior citizens and infants, arrived at Hyderabad's Rajiv Gandhi International Airport to board a flight to Mysore. Less than three hours before departure, the airline sent an SMS notifying them of the flight's cancellation. Left stranded without assistance or refreshments, the passengers were offered alternate seats only for a few members of the group, which they could not take. Alliance Air then issued a written communication advising them to cancel their trip entirely. The cancellation resulted in a forfeiture of ₹2.70 lakh spent on non-refundable hotel stays in Ooty and Mudumalai, alongside pre-booked cab rentals. By an order dated July 11, 2024, the Commission held Alliance Air guilty of gross deficiency in service and non-compliance with Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) passenger care norms. The carrier was directed to pay ₹2.70 lakh towards actual financial losses, ₹9.90 lakh in aggregate compensation (₹30,000 per passenger), and ₹20,000 in litigation costs within 45 days, failing which the awarded amount would attract 12% annual interest. The complaint against Air India was dismissed as it was a distinct corporate entity after its privatisation. When the airline failed to satisfy the award, the consumers filed an execution plea. On August 25 this year, the Commission dismissed the airline’s Section 317 CrPC application seeking exemption from personal appearance, observed continued non-compliance and issued NBWs against the airline. Following the coercive order, the carrier delivered a demand draft covering the entire decretal sum along with accrued default interest, taking the total payout past ₹16 lakh. items.title: Democracy must allow its citizens to question the government: CM DK Shivakumar at NLSIU
items.summary: Karnataka Chief Minister DK Shivakumar on Saturday said that a strong democracy is not one where everyone agrees with the government but one which allows its citizens to question the government. At a time when democratic institutions across the world are facing challenges, young lawyers and policymakers have a special responsibility to protect the Constitution and uphold democratic values, he opined. “A strong democracy must allow its citizens to question the government. A strong democracy is not one where everyone agrees with the government. It is one where every citizen has the freedom to question the government. Never stop questioning, never compromise on your values and never forget the people,” he said. Shivakumar was addressing graduating students at the 34th convocation ceremony of the National Law School of India University (NLSIU) at the Jnana Jyothi Auditorium in Bengaluru. He urged law graduates to question, debate and challenge ideas while also taking responsibility for finding solutions. Constitutional principles, he said, must not remain confined to textbooks but should guide governance, policymaking and public life. “India does not merely need more lawyers. We need lawyers with integrity, compassion and courage. You must understand the struggles of ordinary people and speak up for what is right, however difficult it may be,” he told the graduates. The CM also announced that the Karnataka government would establish a dedicated institution to train law graduates for judicial services examinations and provide continuing education to young lawyers. The government would also support the establishment of a start-up law clinic at NLSIU, where students, faculty members and lawyers would offer pro bono legal advice to young entrepreneurs, he said. Shivakumar also flagged the issue of pendency in courts and highlighted that crores of cases remain pending before Indian courts, leaving individuals and families waiting for justice. “What may be just another case number for us could be someone's entire life. It is essential to make justice faster, simpler, affordable and accessible to everyone,” he said. He said India's goal of becoming a developed nation by 2047 should not be measured merely through economic growth, infrastructure and employment, but also through the dignity, liberty, equality and security enjoyed by its citizens. items.title: Children too have fundamental right to access internet; can't deny it citing online harm: Supreme Court
items.summary: The Supreme Court has held that children have a fundamental right to access and use the internet and protecting them from online harm cannot justify denying them access altogether [Just Rights for Children Alliance & Anr. v. S. Harish & Ors.]. A Bench of Justices JB Pardiwala and K Vinod Chandran passed the order while issuing extensive directions to detect and remove child sexual exploitation and abuse material (CSEAM) online. The Court said that internet access, as a fundamental right under Article 21 read with Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution, is available to children as well as adults. “We have no hesitation in saying that the right to access and use the internet is a fundamental right of every individual under Article 21 read with Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution. Our children, irrespective of their age enjoy the same rights, and to deny the same altogether would be as absurd as saying children below a certain age do not have a conscience worth protecting or a freedom of speech worth expressing. The safety of our children and their freedom are not at odds with each other. Our children are entitled to both, ” the Court said in its order passed on 15 October. Our children, irrespective of their age enjoy the same rights. The Court reasoned that measures intended to protect children must target harmful material and those responsible for it, rather than children themselves. In cases involving CSEAM, the wrongdoers are those who create, circulate, sell or seek out such material, and intermediaries that fail to detect and remove it, the Bench said. “ To keep the child away from the internet on account of such failures would be to mistake the victim for the problem, ” it added. items.title: Detained on arrival: Section 172 BNSS and the borrowed power to stop a protest
items.summary: On October 10, 2026, a protest at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar was supposed to take place. For many who set out to participate in this protest, the trip was cut short on the railway platform itself. People travelling to Delhi for the protest were reportedly detained in several States before they even reached the capital. In Madhya Pradesh, at least 30 people were taken off trains and were detained at Bhopal, Gwalior and Itarsi . In Delhi itself, the police had imposed prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS), which bars assemblies of five or more, processions and dharnas without prior written permission. None of this is new. What is new is the provision the State now uses to justify it. When the Uttarakhand High Court asked, in July, under what law an activist on his way to an earlier protest at Jantar Mantar had been taken off a train at Rishikesh, the State’s answer was Section 172 of the BNSS. That answer deserves scrutiny, because Section 172 does not carry the power it is being asked to carry. It is a power to enforce a police officer’s own directions within one narrow chapter of the Sanhita. It is being used to enforce a magistrate’s order made under another chapter, against the people who have not even reached the place that the order covers. A new power with a narrow door Section 172(1) binds all persons to “conform to the lawful directions of a police officer given in fulfilment of any of his duty under this Chapter.” Section 172(2) allows the officer to “detain or remove” anyone “resisting, refusing, ignoring or disregarding” such a direction, and then either take that person before a magistrate or, “in petty cases”, release them within 24 hours. The previous statute, the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, had no equivalent provision. Detention for disobeying a police direction is a new addition in the BNSS. The operative phrase is “under this Chapter”. Section 172 is present in Chapter XII , “Preventive Action of the Police”, which runs from Section 168 to Section 172. The duties it contains are: to prevent cognizable offences (Section 168), to pass on information of a design to commit one (Section 169), to arrest where that design is known and the offence cannot otherwise be prevented (Section 170) and to prevent injury to public property (Section 171). items.title: The void marriage and the invisible widow: Why the law needs an equitable answer
items.summary: A woman can spend her adult life with a man, raise his children, run his household and give up her career, and still walk away with nothing the day he dies, because a court later finds the marriage void. This recurs whenever a marriage falls foul of Section 5, read with Section 11, of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 (HMA). The woman never becomes a wife in the eyes of law, so she can never become a widow either. And the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 (HSA) has no room for her. The answer is not to pretend the marriage was valid. It lies in something the HMA already accepts: that the legal fate of a relationship and its economic consequences need not be tied together. Section 16 legitimises children of void and voidable marriages without validating the marriage. The same idea can be extended, carefully and narrowly, to the woman who lived the marriage in good faith. The statutory bind Section 5(i) requires that neither party have a living spouse at the time of marriage. Section 11 declares a marriage in breach void from inception (Section 12 covers voidable marriages), so the woman never becomes a wife. Section 8 of the HSA sends a Hindu male's intestate property first to his Class I heirs, which include the widow. But “widow” assumes a marriage that existed and ended in death. The Supreme Court said so in Rameshwari Devi v. State of Bihar (2000) where the second wife of a man whose earlier marriage was subsisting was denied any share as a widow. As statutory construction, this is unimpeachable. The problem is what follows: the woman is left with no legal identity in relation to the man she lived with for years, sometimes decades. What Section 16 already teaches us In Revanasiddappa v. Mallikarjun (2023) , a three-judge bench held that children of void and voidable marriages, legitimised by Section 16, are entitled to their parents' property, including the share the parent would get on a notional partition of coparcenary property. While such children do not become coparceners by birth, they cannot be denied that share once it crystallises. This departs from the stricter position in Jinia Keotin v. Kumar Sitaram Manjhi (2003) , which confined such children to self-acquired property. items.title: The long wait: What 24 Supreme Court references reveal about judicial delay
items.summary: In February 2002, seven judges of the Supreme Court were asked whether a citizen’s private property counts as a “material resource of the community” that the State may redistribute under Article 39(b). The Court said it had “some difficulty” with an older ruling answering the question in the affirmative and sent the question to nine judges. Those nine judges first sat on April 23, 2024. The judgment in Property Owners Association v. State of Maharashtra was pronounced on November 5, 2024. 22 years and nine months to get a hearing. Six-and-a-half months to decide. I wanted to know whether that was unusual, so I counted. I collected every question the Supreme Court sent to a bench of seven or more judges that was decided, or was still waiting, between January 2000 and September 30, 2026. There are 24. The dates come from the judgments, the Supreme Court Observer’s case records and the list the Law Ministry placed before the Lok Sabha in July 2023. What I found is not a story about one slow case. It is a story about how the Court runs. First, how this works Two rules explain everything that follows. The first is that a bench of the Supreme Court cannot overrule a decision given by a bench of the same size or bigger. If three judges think an old five-judge ruling is wrong, they cannot simply say so. They must pass an order sending the question to a bench of seven or more. The process is generally called a reference . Any bench can make one. The second rule is about what happens next. Someone has to pick seven or nine judges, take them off their regular work and fix a date. Under the Court’s own judgments, from Campaign for Judicial Accountability and Reforms v. Union of India (2017) to Shanti Bhushan v. Supreme Court of India (2018) , only the Chief Justice can do that as “master of the roster”. A referring bench can request an early hearing. It cannot order one. And nothing in the Supreme Court Rules says that a reference must be heard within any time at all. How long they waited Of the 19 references that have been decided in this period, half waited more than 5.7 years. Six waited more than 12. The five still pending have waited 3.4, 6.9, 6.9, 21.8 and 27 years. The oldest is Arjun Flour Mills v. State of Orissa , n whether States can add a surcharge to sales tax. items.title: YSRCP tells SC violence stopped candidates from filing nomination for local body polls
items.summary: The Yuvajana Sramika Rythu Congress Party (YSRCP) approached the Supreme Court on Monday, October 19, challenging an October 18 order of the Andhra Pradesh High Court that refused to extend the deadline for filing nominations for the ongoing Urban Local Body (ULB) elections, which expired on the same day. The party alleges that violence and intimidation in Andhra Pradesh prevented several of its candidates from filing nominations. In a special leave petition filed through its General Secretary Lella Appireddy, YSRCP is seeking an extension of the nomination period, police protection for its candidates, and the designation of additional or alternative nomination centres to enable them to file papers safely. It is also seeking a stay on the declaration of candidates as elected unopposed in the affected wards. The petition alleges that several YSRCP candidates were assaulted, threatened, or physically prevented from reaching nomination centres during the nomination period, which ran from October 16 to 18. The party cites such incidents in Punganur, Rayachoti, Kadapa, and Tirupati. The petition alleges that the nomination papers of a candidate in Kadapa were snatched and torn. It also states that nine candidates contesting the Tirupati Municipal Corporation elections were prevented from entering the offices of the concerned Returning Officers. The party further alleges that the convoy of YSRCP MP PV Midhun Reddy was attacked while he was accompanying candidates to file their nominations. The YSRCP had earlier approached the Andhra Pradesh High Court seeking additional nomination facilities at district headquarters, citing apprehensions of violence. On October 15, a single judge declined to grant the blanket relief sought by the party but gave individual candidates the liberty to approach the concerned Election Officers. Following the alleged incidents on October 16, the party approached the State Election Commission seeking an extension of the nomination deadline. According to the petition, the Commission directed that adequate security be provided at nomination centres but did not extend the deadline. The YSRCP subsequently approached the High Court again, seeking an extension by one day. However, in its October 18 order, the High Court dismissed the plea, holding that the nomination period had expired and that extending it would amount to interference in the election process. items.title: Rishikanth, female fandom and the fine line between desire and objectification
items.summary: It has been nearly two months since Modha Rathri and 25 days since Dorothy were released. For actor Rishikanth, who starred in both, life hasn't been the same. It has swung from online and offline adoration to what can well be termed harassment in the public space. Rishi’s screen presence as Marudhu and Karthi in the two films has brought in comparisons with Rajinikanth. There’s joy that a Tamil-looking hero is making it big on screen, and he’s receiving overwhelming love from female audiences. However, his boundaries have been quashed, and he’s being seen as a commodity – squished, scratched, hugged forcibly, so much so that on occasions, the team handling him had to pull him up from the thronging crowd and peel female fans off him. Quite a few social media posts border on insensitivity and sexual innuendo. Close-ups have been posted of his stretch marks and shoulder scar and of his ‘bedroom eyes’. This all sounds eerily similar to how heroines have, for decades, been objectified in print and now online — from morphed images to insensitive AI-generated videos (the latest involved Janhvi Kapoor from the Dasara song ‘Chuttamalle’) — and sometimes seen it spill over to real life, with stalking, chasing and break-ins. So, when we raise our voices against those perpetrators, must we not do the same when the victim happens to be a male? The last time girls and women in Tamil Nadu went crazy about an actor was in 1992, after Roja was released and actor Arvind Swami happened. There was no social media, and all people depended on were news clippings and the rare song on TV to spot an actor who was unlike anything they’d seen before, in films or real life. He spoke perfect English and played a collector and an IT guy in two of his movies… He was an aspiration of what several women wanted their perfect man to be. It was the kind of fandom some might dream of. But Arvind has often spoken about how all that attention made him feel very uncomfortable, and he wanted people to see his film but leave him alone. “If I came out and saw 100 people standing, it would make some people happy and proud or make some people run back to their house. I belong to the second category," he was quoted as saying by PTI in 2016.
